opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to understand it is that rule-based reinforcement learning doesn't really teach the model new knowledge. It's more like it activates, or selects, abilities that are already latent in the pretrained model.

When you pretrain on an enormous corpus, the model has seen a huge number of reasoning patterns: people working through math problems, checking their own work, saying "wait, that's wrong, let me try again." All of that is in the data, but it's mixed in with a lot of noise and shallow pattern-matching. So the pretrained model has the capacity for long, careful reasoning, but it doesn't reliably choose to use it.

What rule-based RL does is give a very clean, very hard-to-game signal. Is the final answer correct or not? Does the code pass the tests or not? Because the reward comes from a verifier rather than a learned reward model, there's much less room for reward hacking. The model can't just learn to sound convincing; it actually has to get the answer right. Under that pressure, the behaviors that genuinely help, like reflection, backtracking, trying multiple approaches, and spending more tokens on harder problems, get reinforced, and the ones that don't help get suppressed.

That's why you see this phenomenon where the response length grows during training and these "aha moment" behaviors emerge. People sometimes describe it as emergence from nothing, but I'd say it's emergence from a strong prior. If you run the same recipe on a weak base model, you don't get much. The base model has to be good enough that, when it samples, it occasionally stumbles onto a correct chain of reasoning. RL then amplifies those occasional successes.

So my view is: pretraining determines the ceiling, and rule-based RL is a very efficient way to push the model toward that ceiling, especially in domains where correctness can be checked. The open question for me is how far this extends beyond math and code, into areas where you can't write a simple rule to decide what's right. That's where I think a lot of the interesting research will be.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to understand it is that pretraining and rule-based reinforcement learning are doing two very different jobs, and the division of labor matters more than people sometimes assume.

Pretraining puts almost all of the knowledge and the capability into the model. When you train on trillions of tokens, the model has already seen the reasoning patterns, the math, the code, the ways humans correct themselves. All of that is latent in the weights. The problem is that the model doesn't know which of those behaviors to prefer. It's a very broad distribution over possible behaviors, and the good behaviors are in there, but so are a lot of mediocre ones.

What rule-based RL does, in my view, is select rather than teach. With a verifiable reward, whether the answer to a math problem is correct or whether the code passes the test, you get a very clean, very hard-to-game signal. You don't need a learned reward model that might have its own biases or get exploited. The model samples many trajectories, and you simply reinforce the ones that worked. Over time, the model sharpens its own distribution toward the behaviors that lead to correct outcomes, things like checking its work, backtracking, trying a second approach when the first one stalls. We often say the model "learned to reason," but I think it's closer to say it learned to reliably express a reasoning ability that pretraining already gave it.

That's why I think it only works well on a heavily pretrained base. If the base is weak, the probability of ever sampling a correct trajectory is too low, the reward is almost always zero, and there's nothing to reinforce. The stronger the base, the more RL has to work with. So in a sense, the quality of pretraining is the ceiling, and RL is how you actually reach that ceiling.

There are limits, of course. Rule-based rewards only exist where you can verify things, so math, code, some logic tasks. For open-ended writing or judgment, you still need something else. And the gains don't come from nowhere. If the model never learns a fact in pretraining, RL won't invent it. But within the domains where you can verify, I think it's one of the most efficient tools we have, because it's precise, scalable, and very hard to fool.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate where the model’s capabilities come from from how we make those capabilities useful. A heavily pretrained language model already has a broad repertoire of knowledge and reasoning patterns. Rule-based reinforcement learning gives it a clear signal about which behaviors lead to a successful result.

For example, if a mathematical answer can be checked, or a piece of code can be tested, we can use those checks as rewards. We don’t necessarily have to specify every intermediate step. The model can explore different approaches and become more likely to produce ones that pass the check.

But a higher reward doesn’t automatically mean the model has acquired a fundamentally new reasoning ability. It might be using an existing ability more consistently. With further exploration and training, it may also develop strategies that were previously very unlikely. Distinguishing those possibilities requires more than looking at a benchmark score.

So I see rule-based reinforcement learning as a powerful way to build on pretraining, especially where correctness is verifiable. Its limitation is that the model learns to satisfy the rule we actually implement. If that rule is incomplete, improving the reward can diverge from improving what we really care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate where the model’s capabilities come from from how we make those capabilities useful. After extensive pretraining, a language model already has a broad repertoire of knowledge and behaviors. Reinforcement learning with rule-based rewards can encourage it to select behaviors that succeed on a particular task.

For example, in mathematics or coding, we can often check whether an answer is correct or whether a program passes tests. That gives us a relatively clear training signal without requiring a person to judge every response. The model explores different solutions, and successful ones become more likely.

But a correct answer doesn’t necessarily mean the reasoning is sound, and passing tests doesn’t mean a program is universally correct. The model can also exploit weaknesses in the reward. So the verifier matters enormously.

I’d view this kind of reinforcement learning as a way to refine and potentially extend a pretrained model’s problem-solving behavior. It’s too strong to say it only reveals capabilities that were already there, but it’s also misleading to attribute all the resulting intelligence to reinforcement learning. The pretrained foundation, the tasks, and the reward design work together.
